rationale:
The requirement states a signature (`NodePath::new(Vec<String>)`, `segments(&self) -> &[String]`), an ordered-sequence meaning, private fields, and seven trait implementations (Clone, Debug, Deserialize, Hash, PartialEq, Serialize, Eq). The tests cover each of these.

- **`new` and `segments` keep the order and content of the segments.** `crates/trust-but-verify/tests/contracts.rs#fn[node_paths_round_trip_empty_and_separated_segments]` builds paths from `[]`, `[""]`, `["a/b"]` and `["a","b"]`. It asserts that `segments()` equals the input after a serde round trip. `src/sdk.rs#mod[tests]/fn[habeas_paths_preserve_opaque_segments_and_separate_all_node_kinds]` asserts exact `segments()` values for every node kind.
- **Order matters.** `identities_remain_stable_and_fingerprinting_uses_the_supplied_snapshot` asserts that `["a","b"]` is not equal to `["b","a"]`. It also checks that case, whitespace, separator and Unicode-normalization differences, and `[]` against `[""]` against `["",""]`, give unequal paths.
- **Serialize and Deserialize.** The JSON round trip in the first test serializes and deserializes, then asserts `decoded == path`.
- **Clone, PartialEq and Eq.** The stability test asserts `path == path.clone()`. It also asserts inequality across the whole path set.
- **Hash and Eq.** The sdk test inserts many paths into a `HashSet`, which requires both traits. It asserts that distinct paths are all accepted. Rebuilt equal paths are checked with `assert_eq!`.
- **Debug.** `assert_eq!`/`assert_ne!` require `Debug`, so the trait is exercised at compile time.
- **Private fields.** The `compile_fail` doctest on `NodePath` in `crates/trust-but-verify/src/graph.rs#struct[NodePath]` checks that the fields are inaccessible. `public_exports_match_the_appendix` checks the exports.

The trait implementations are plain derives with no conditional logic of their own. I found no obligation left untested, and I did not request implementation source.

text: `trust_but_verify::graph::NodePath` describes a node identity as an ordered sequence of path segments.
